cards.q: From what precursor molecule are all steroid hormones synthesized?
cards.a: Cholesterol.
options: Cholesterol
Tyrosine
A ribosomal peptide chain
Arachidonic acid
cards.explanation: Every steroid hormone starts as cholesterol and is modified by a series of enzymes in the smooth endoplasmic reticulum and mitochondria, which is why the steroids all share a similar four ring core. Tyrosine is the precursor for the amine hormones, including thyroid hormone and the catecholamines. A ribosomal peptide chain is how peptide hormones begin, and arachidonic acid gives rise to eicosanoids, which are local paracrines rather than steroid hormones.

cards.q: Where does synthesis of a peptide hormone begin in the endocrine cell?
cards.a: On ribosomes of the rough endoplasmic reticulum.
options: In the smooth endoplasmic reticulum and mitochondria
On ribosomes of the rough endoplasmic reticulum
In the mitochondrial matrix
In the cytosol from cholesterol
cards.explanation: Peptide hormones are proteins, so they are translated on rough ER ribosomes as a preprohormone and then trimmed in the ER and Golgi before packaging. The smooth ER and the mitochondria are the sites where steroid synthesis enzymes work. Cholesterol in the cytosol is a steroid precursor, not a template for a peptide sequence.

cards.q: How is a peptide hormone handled between synthesis and secretion?
cards.a: It is stored in secretory vesicles until a signal causes exocytosis.
options: It is stored in the nucleus bound to DNA
It diffuses out of the cell as fast as it is made, with no storage
It is stored in secretory vesicles until a signal causes exocytosis
It is bound to cholesterol and held in lipid droplets in the cytosol
cards.explanation: Because peptides are water soluble they cannot cross the membrane, so the cell packages them in vesicles and releases a preformed pool by exocytosis, which allows a fast burst of secretion. Immediate diffusion out of the cell describes steroid release, since steroids are lipid soluble. Lipid droplets store cholesterol esters as raw material, not finished peptide, and hormones are not stored on DNA.

cards.q: How much steroid hormone does a steroid secreting cell keep in storage?
cards.a: Almost none, since steroids leave as fast as they are made.
options: A week of supply bound to intracellular receptors in the cell
A pool held in the Golgi until a neural signal arrives
A large vesicle pool that is released by exocytosis on demand
Almost none, since steroids leave as fast as they are made
cards.explanation: Steroids are lipid soluble, so they cross the plasma membrane the moment they are made and cannot be held in a vesicle. Secretion rate therefore tracks synthesis rate, and the controlled step is the enzyme that converts cholesterol to pregnenolone. Vesicle pools and Golgi storage are features of peptide hormones, and intracellular receptors are in target cells, not storage sites in the gland.

cards.q: Where is the receptor for a peptide hormone located?
cards.a: On the outer surface of the target cell plasma membrane.
options: On the outer surface of the target cell plasma membrane
On the inner face of the mitochondrial membrane
In the nucleus bound to a response element
Free in the cytosol
cards.explanation: A peptide hormone is water soluble and cannot cross the lipid bilayer, so its receptor must face the extracellular fluid and pass the message inward through a second messenger. Nuclear and cytosolic receptors belong to the lipid soluble hormones that can enter the cell. The mitochondrial membrane is not a hormone receptor site in this scheme.

cards.q: Where is the receptor for a steroid hormone located?
cards.a: Inside the cell, in the cytosol or the nucleus.
options: In the extracellular matrix next to the cell
Inside the cell, in the cytosol or the nucleus
On the plasma membrane coupled to a G protein
On the plasma membrane with tyrosine kinase activity
cards.explanation: Steroids are lipid soluble and diffuse through the bilayer, so the receptor waits inside and the hormone receptor complex acts on DNA to change transcription. G protein coupled and tyrosine kinase receptors sit in the membrane and serve water soluble hormones such as epinephrine and insulin. Nothing in the extracellular matrix serves as a hormone receptor here.

cards.q: Amine hormones are synthesized by modifying which amino acid?
cards.a: Tyrosine.
options: Glycine
Tryptophan
Tyrosine
Glutamate
cards.explanation: Both families of amine hormones taught here, the thyroid hormones and the catecholamines, are built from tyrosine, which is why the two look chemically related despite behaving very differently. Tryptophan is the precursor for serotonin and melatonin, which are amines but not the endocrine examples used for this competency. Glycine and glutamate act as neurotransmitters and are not hormone precursors.

cards.q: Insulin, cortisol, and epinephrine belong to which classes, in that order?
cards.a: Peptide, steroid, amine.
options: Amine, steroid, peptide
Peptide, amine, steroid
Steroid, peptide, amine
Peptide, steroid, amine
cards.explanation: Insulin is a chain of amino acids, cortisol is built from cholesterol in the adrenal cortex, and epinephrine is a small molecule made from tyrosine in the adrenal medulla. Calling insulin a steroid misses that it is destroyed by digestion and must be injected. Swapping cortisol and epinephrine confuses the adrenal cortex, which makes steroids, with the adrenal medulla, which makes catecholamines.

cards.q: A hormone binds a receptor inside the nucleus and changes the rate of transcription of specific genes. Which class is it most likely to be?
cards.a: Steroid.
options: Steroid
Catecholamine
Prostaglandin
Peptide
cards.explanation: Only a lipid soluble hormone can reach an intranuclear receptor, and steroid is the class defined by that route, so the response is a change in the amount of new protein made. Peptides and catecholamines act at surface receptors and change the activity of proteins already present. Prostaglandins are local eicosanoids and are not part of the three class hormone scheme.

cards.q: A drug blocks all new gene transcription in a target cell. Which hormone response is blocked first?
cards.a: Cortisol raising the amount of gluconeogenic enzyme.
options: Epinephrine activating existing glycogen phosphorylase
Cortisol raising the amount of gluconeogenic enzyme
Insulin causing existing glucose transporters to move to the membrane
Glucagon raising cyclic AMP in a liver cell
cards.explanation: A steroid works by making new messenger RNA and new protein, so blocking transcription removes its whole mechanism. The other three act through second messengers on proteins the cell already has, which is why their effects appear within seconds and survive a transcription block. Those responses would eventually fade if the cell could never replace worn proteins, but that is a much slower effect.

cards.q: Why must insulin be injected rather than swallowed?
cards.a: It is a peptide and would be digested into amino acids in the gut.
options: It binds an intracellular receptor that the gut lining does not have
It is a steroid and would be stored in fat before reaching the blood
It is a peptide and would be digested into amino acids in the gut
It is an amine and would be destroyed by stomach acid into cholesterol
cards.explanation: Peptide hormones are proteins, and the digestive tract breaks proteins into amino acids, so an oral dose never arrives intact at the target. Steroids are the class that survives the gut and can be taken as a pill, which is why prednisone works orally. Insulin is not an amine, and the reason has nothing to do with receptor location, since insulin receptors are on the cell surface.

cards.q: A newly described hormone is lipid soluble, is not stored in the gland, and can be taken as a tablet. Which class fits best?
cards.a: Steroid.
options: Glycoprotein
Peptide
Catecholamine
Steroid
cards.explanation: Lipid solubility explains all three observations at once: the molecule leaves the cell as soon as it is made, so there is no storage pool, and it crosses the gut lining intact, so it survives an oral dose. Peptides and glycoproteins are water soluble, stored in vesicles, and digested if swallowed. Catecholamines are water soluble as well and act at surface receptors with a very short life in plasma.

cards.q: Thyroid hormone is built from tyrosine, yet it uses an intracellular receptor. Which property explains that?
cards.a: It is lipid soluble, so it can cross the plasma membrane.
options: It is lipid soluble, so it can cross the plasma membrane
It is a large glycoprotein that is taken in by endocytosis
It is made from cholesterol despite its name
It is stored in vesicles like a peptide
cards.explanation: Receptor location follows solubility, not the precursor, and thyroid hormone is lipid soluble enough to enter the cell and act on nuclear receptors like a steroid. That is why its effects are slow to start and long lasting. It is not a glycoprotein, and it is built from tyrosine and iodine rather than from cholesterol. Its storage is unusual, held extracellularly in thyroid colloid rather than in secretory vesicles.

cards.q: Two hormones reach a cell at the same instant. One acts within seconds, the other over hours. What most likely accounts for the difference?
cards.a: The fast one changes existing proteins, the slow one makes new protein.
options: The fast one is carried bound to plasma protein, the slow one travels free
The fast one changes existing proteins, the slow one makes new protein
The fast one is present at a higher concentration in blood
The fast one is larger, so it binds its receptor more tightly
cards.explanation: A surface receptor and a second messenger can phosphorylate enzymes that are already in the cell, which takes seconds, while transcription, translation, and protein accumulation take hours. Binding to plasma protein changes half life and free fraction, not the speed of the intracellular step. Concentration and molecular size shift potency and clearance but do not explain a difference measured in hours.

cards.q: A gland is treated with a drug that blocks exocytosis. Secretion of which hormone is affected least?
cards.a: Cortisol from the adrenal cortex.
options: Insulin from the pancreatic beta cell
Growth hormone from the anterior pituitary
Cortisol from the adrenal cortex
Antidiuretic hormone from the posterior pituitary
cards.explanation: Cortisol is a steroid, so it leaves by simple diffusion through the membrane as soon as it is synthesized and never enters a vesicle. Insulin, growth hormone, and antidiuretic hormone are all peptides held in secretory vesicles, so blocking exocytosis traps them inside the cell. Steroid secretion is instead limited by the enzymes that convert cholesterol into the hormone.

cards.q: An enzyme that converts cholesterol to pregnenolone is inhibited in the adrenal cortex. Predict the effect on stored hormone available for immediate release and on the plasma level over the next hour.
cards.a: There is no stored pool, so plasma cortisol falls as synthesis stops.
options: Plasma cortisol rises because the blocked precursor is diverted to hormone
Plasma cortisol is unchanged because cortisol is recycled from target cells
A vesicle pool sustains normal plasma levels for several hours
There is no stored pool, so plasma cortisol falls as synthesis stops
cards.explanation: Steroid secreting cells store almost no finished hormone, so output equals synthesis and a block early in the pathway shows up in the blood within minutes to an hour. A vesicle buffer of several hours is what you would see if you blocked synthesis of a peptide hormone instead. Blocking a step cannot increase product downstream of the block, and hormones are cleared by the liver and kidney rather than recycled back to the gland.

cards.q: A researcher labels an endocrine cell and finds abundant rough endoplasmic reticulum, a large Golgi, and many dense secretory granules. The hormone it makes acts on target cells within seconds. Where is its receptor and why?
cards.a: On the cell surface, because a water soluble peptide cannot cross the membrane.
options: On the cell surface, because a water soluble peptide cannot cross the membrane
In the cytosol, because the hormone is lipid soluble
On the target cell surface, because the hormone is a steroid released by exocytosis
In the nucleus, because rapid effects require new transcription
cards.explanation: Heavy protein synthesis machinery plus dense granules identifies a peptide hormone, and a water soluble peptide has to signal from outside, which also fits the response within seconds. New transcription is the slow route and would not give a seconds long latency. Cytosolic receptors require lipid solubility, and steroids are never released by exocytosis because they are not packaged.

cards.q: A patient is given a drug that inhibits protein synthesis in liver cells. Predict the effect on the immediate glucose releasing action of glucagon and on the slower glucose raising action of cortisol.
cards.a: The glucagon effect is preserved and the cortisol effect is lost.
options: Both effects are lost, since both hormones act on the liver
The glucagon effect is preserved and the cortisol effect is lost
The cortisol effect is preserved and the glucagon effect is lost
Both effects are preserved, since the drug acts only in the gland
cards.explanation: Glucagon works through cyclic AMP and protein kinase A on enzymes the liver cell already contains, so it does not need the ribosome, while cortisol raises glucose by increasing the amount of gluconeogenic enzyme, which requires new protein. Losing both would only happen if the drug also blocked second messenger signaling. Reversing the two mixes up surface receptor speed with nuclear receptor speed.

cards.q: Iodine is removed from the diet of an experimental animal. Trace the effect through synthesis to the class of hormone affected.
cards.a: Amine synthesis in the thyroid falls, because iodine is added to tyrosine.
options: Catecholamine synthesis in the adrenal medulla falls, because epinephrine contains iodine
Steroid synthesis falls, because iodine is needed to convert cholesterol to pregnenolone
Amine synthesis in the thyroid falls, because iodine is added to tyrosine
Peptide hormone synthesis falls, because iodine is a required amino acid
cards.explanation: Thyroid hormone is a tyrosine based amine whose activity depends on the iodine atoms attached to it, so no iodine means no functional hormone. Steroid synthesis uses cholesterol and needs no iodine. Iodine is not an amino acid and does not limit peptide synthesis, and the catecholamines, though also built from tyrosine, contain no iodine.

cards.q: Which fraction of a circulating hormone is able to bind target cell receptors?
cards.a: The free, unbound fraction.
options: The fraction bound to albumin only
The total of bound plus free
The fraction bound to carrier protein
The free, unbound fraction
cards.explanation: Only unbound hormone can leave the capillary and reach a receptor, so the free fraction sets the biological effect no matter how large the total is. Hormone held by a carrier, including albumin, is chemically shielded and inactive until it dissociates. Total hormone is what most simple blood tests report, which is exactly why total and activity can disagree.

cards.q: Which hormone classes travel through plasma mostly bound to carrier proteins?
cards.a: Steroid and thyroid hormones.
options: Steroid and thyroid hormones
Only the catecholamines
Only the glycoprotein hormones
Peptide and catecholamine hormones
cards.explanation: Steroid and thyroid hormones are lipid soluble and poorly soluble in water, so they need a protein carrier to stay dissolved and to travel any distance in plasma. Peptides and catecholamines are water soluble and dissolve directly in plasma, circulating mostly free. Glycoproteins such as TSH are large water soluble peptides, so they too need no carrier.

cards.q: What is the approximate plasma half life of a typical peptide hormone?
cards.a: A few minutes.
options: A few seconds
A few minutes
About one day
About one week
cards.explanation: Peptides circulate free, are filtered at the kidney, and are cleaved by plasma and tissue peptidases, which gives them a half life on the order of minutes and lets their levels change quickly. A few seconds is closer to the catecholamines, which are cleared even faster. A day to a week describes the protein bound hormones, with thyroxine at the long end.

cards.q: Which hormone has the longest plasma half life of these four?
cards.a: Thyroxine, T4.
options: Epinephrine
Insulin
Thyroxine, T4
Antidiuretic hormone
cards.explanation: Thyroxine is almost entirely bound to thyroxine binding globulin and other plasma proteins, so it is protected from clearance and lasts about a week, which is why thyroid hormone levels change slowly. Epinephrine lasts seconds, and insulin and antidiuretic hormone last minutes, since all three circulate free and are cleared rapidly. Binding, not gland size, is the reason for the difference.

cards.q: Which plasma protein carries the largest share of cortisol?
cards.a: Corticosteroid binding globulin.
options: Sex hormone binding globulin
Hemoglobin
Thyroxine binding globulin
Corticosteroid binding globulin
cards.explanation: Corticosteroid binding globulin, also called transcortin, is the high affinity carrier for cortisol, with albumin taking a smaller share. Thyroxine binding globulin carries thyroid hormone and sex hormone binding globulin carries testosterone and estradiol, each named for its cargo. Hemoglobin is inside red cells and carries respiratory gases, not hormones.

cards.q: How does binding to a plasma carrier protein change the clearance of a hormone?
cards.a: It slows clearance by hiding hormone from filtration and enzymes.
options: It slows clearance by hiding hormone from filtration and enzymes
It speeds clearance by delivering the hormone to the liver faster
It has no effect, since only total hormone matters
It speeds clearance by making the hormone easier to filter
cards.explanation: A hormone bound to a large protein cannot pass the glomerular filter and is hidden from degrading enzymes, so it persists and the carrier acts as a circulating reservoir. Carriers do not target hormone to the liver for destruction. Total hormone does not set activity, and the bound complex is too large to filter, which is the opposite of easier filtration.

cards.q: Besides prolonging half life, what is the main transport reason a lipid soluble hormone needs a carrier protein?
cards.a: It is poorly soluble in the watery plasma on its own.
options: It would otherwise be too large to enter a capillary
It is poorly soluble in the watery plasma on its own
It would otherwise bind its receptor before reaching the target
It carries a strong negative charge that plasma cannot buffer
cards.explanation: Plasma is water, and a lipid soluble molecule will not stay dissolved in it at useful concentrations, so the carrier keeps the hormone in solution while it travels. Steroids are small molecules, so size is not the barrier. Receptors are on target tissues rather than floating in blood, and steroids are not strongly charged.

cards.q: What relationship links free hormone and bound hormone in plasma?
cards.a: They are in reversible equilibrium, so bound hormone replaces free.
options: Free hormone can only be replaced by new secretion from the gland
Binding is irreversible, so bound hormone is permanently lost
They are in reversible equilibrium, so bound hormone replaces free
Bound hormone converts to a different hormone before release
cards.explanation: Carrier binding obeys mass action, so as target tissues take up free hormone the complex dissociates and buffers the free concentration, smoothing out swings between secretory bursts. Irreversible binding would make the bound pool useless as a reserve. No chemical conversion happens on the carrier, and the reserve means the gland is not the only source of replacement over the short term.

cards.q: A drug displaces cortisol from corticosteroid binding globulin. What happens to the free cortisol concentration immediately after the drug is given?
cards.a: It rises.
options: It falls
It is unchanged
It falls, then total cortisol falls with it
It rises
cards.explanation: Displacement moves hormone from the bound reserve into the free pool, so free cortisol rises at once and biological activity increases before feedback has time to respond. It cannot fall, because nothing is being removed from the plasma. Saying it is unchanged confuses total hormone, which barely moves at first, with the free fraction that actually acts.

cards.q: Pregnancy raises thyroxine binding globulin in plasma. What happens to total thyroxine in a woman whose thyroid gland is healthy?
cards.a: Total T4 rises while free T4 stays near normal.
options: Total T4 rises while free T4 stays near normal
Both total and free T4 fall
Both total and free T4 rise well above normal
Total T4 falls while free T4 rises
cards.explanation: More carrier binds more hormone, so the total measured in plasma goes up, but feedback adjusts secretion until the free level is back where it started, which is what the hypothalamus and pituitary actually sense. Total falling would require fewer carriers, not more. If free hormone also rose and stayed high, the woman would be thyrotoxic, and negative feedback prevents that in a healthy gland.

cards.q: Liver disease lowers the plasma concentration of hormone binding proteins. Predict the effect on the half life of a highly bound steroid hormone.
cards.a: The half life shortens.
options: The half life lengthens, because less hormone reaches the tissues
The half life shortens
The half life lengthens
The half life is unchanged, since half life depends only on the gland
cards.explanation: Fewer carriers means a larger share of hormone is free and therefore exposed to filtration and enzymatic breakdown, so it disappears from plasma faster. Lengthening would require more binding, not less. Half life is a property of clearance, not of secretion rate, and free hormone reaches tissues more readily rather than less.

cards.q: Two hormones are secreted in equal amounts. Hormone A is 99 percent protein bound, hormone B circulates free. Which shows the more rapid swings in plasma level between secretory bursts?
cards.a: Hormone B, because nothing buffers or protects it.
options: Neither swings, because plasma volume dilutes both
Hormone A, because bound hormone dissociates unpredictably
Hormone B, because nothing buffers or protects it
Both swing equally, since the secretion rate is the same
cards.explanation: A free hormone is cleared quickly and has no reservoir, so its level tracks each burst of secretion and falls just as quickly, which suits hormones that must signal minute to minute. The bound pool of hormone A dissociates in a graded way that buffers the free level rather than making it erratic. Equal secretion rates do not equalize clearance, and plasma dilution applies to both alike.

cards.q: A laboratory reports a normal total thyroxine but the patient has clear signs of thyroid hormone excess. What is the most useful next measurement to explain the discrepancy?
cards.a: Free thyroxine, since only the free fraction acts on tissues.
options: Plasma albumin, since albumin sets total hormone
Urine cholesterol, since thyroxine is made from cholesterol
Total triiodothyronine bound to protein
Free thyroxine, since only the free fraction acts on tissues
cards.explanation: Total hormone lumps the active free fraction together with the much larger inactive bound pool, so a change in carrier protein can hide a real change in what tissues see. Measuring another total value repeats the same problem. Albumin is only a minor carrier for thyroxine, and thyroid hormone is built from tyrosine and iodine, not cholesterol.

cards.q: Which hormone would you expect to be measurable in the urine of a healthy person in the largest proportion of what was secreted?
cards.a: A small water soluble hormone that circulates free.
options: A small water soluble hormone that circulates free
Thyroxine bound to thyroxine binding globulin
A hormone bound to sex hormone binding globulin
A steroid that is 98 percent bound to globulin
cards.explanation: Free hormone is small enough to be filtered at the glomerulus, so an unbound water soluble hormone appears in urine, while carrier bound hormone stays in plasma because the protein cannot cross the filter. The three bound options all describe hormones shielded from filtration. This is the same protection that gives bound hormones their long half lives.

cards.q: A patient starts a drug that competes with thyroxine for binding sites on thyroxine binding globulin. Trace what happens to free T4 immediately and then to total T4 after several days of intact feedback.
cards.a: Free T4 rises at first, then feedback lowers total T4 and free T4 returns to normal.
options: Free T4 falls at first, then total T4 rises as the gland compensates
Free T4 rises at first, then feedback lowers total T4 and free T4 returns to normal
Free and total T4 both rise and stay high, since carrier binding cannot be regulated
Neither value changes, since the carrier only transports hormone
cards.explanation: Displacement shifts hormone into the free pool, and because the hypothalamus and pituitary sense free hormone, TSH falls and secretion drops until free T4 is back near its set point, leaving a lower total in a smaller bound pool. Free T4 cannot fall first, since the drug releases hormone rather than trapping it. Persistent elevation would require the feedback loop to be broken, and a change in binding clearly does change measured values.

cards.q: Hormone X is 99 percent bound with a half life of 7 days. Hormone Y circulates free with a half life of 5 minutes. Which is better suited to controlling a variable that must be corrected within a minute, and why?
cards.a: Hormone Y, because a short half life lets its level rise and fall quickly.
options: Hormone Y, because a long half life allows finer control
Hormone X, because a long half life keeps its concentration reliably high
Hormone Y, because a short half life lets its level rise and fall quickly
Hormone X, because bound hormone is delivered to tissues faster
cards.explanation: Fast control requires that the signal can be turned off as quickly as it was turned on, and only a rapidly cleared hormone can do that, which is why minute to minute regulators such as insulin and epinephrine are short lived. A steady high level is the profile you want for a background setting such as metabolic rate, not for fast correction. Binding slows delivery rather than speeding it, and the choice that credits hormone Y with finer control because it is long lived contradicts its 5 minute half life.

cards.q: After a bolus injection, hormone P disappears from plasma in about 10 minutes while hormone Q takes days. Both are secreted by the same person. What can you conclude about their transport and class?
cards.a: P travels free as a water soluble hormone, Q is lipid soluble and bound.
options: Both must be peptides, since half life depends only on molecular size
P must have a larger secretion rate, which is why it disappears faster
P is likely a steroid carried on globulin, and Q is likely a peptide
P travels free as a water soluble hormone, Q is lipid soluble and bound
cards.explanation: Clearance rate is driven mainly by whether the hormone is shielded by a carrier, so minutes points to a free water soluble hormone and days points to an extensively bound lipid soluble one. Calling P a bound steroid and Q a peptide reverses the two, since steroid binding is what makes a hormone long lived. Size alone does not predict half life, and secretion rate sets concentration rather than the rate of disappearance after injection.

cards.q: A patient with nephrotic syndrome loses large amounts of plasma protein in the urine, including hormone binding globulins. Predict the effect on total cortisol and on free cortisol once feedback has adjusted.
cards.a: Total cortisol falls while free cortisol is held near normal by feedback.
options: Total cortisol falls while free cortisol is held near normal by feedback
Both total and free cortisol fall to very low levels
Both total and free cortisol rise, since less hormone is filtered
Total cortisol rises while free cortisol falls
cards.explanation: Losing carriers shrinks the bound reserve, so the total measured value drops, but the hypothalamic pituitary adrenal axis senses free cortisol and adjusts ACTH until the free level is back at its set point. Total cannot rise when the protein that holds hormone is being lost. A fall in free cortisol to very low levels would require the adrenal gland itself to fail, and protein loss increases rather than decreases filtration of hormone.

cards.q: What determines whether a given cell responds to a hormone circulating in the blood?
cards.a: Whether the cell expresses a receptor for that hormone.
options: Whether the cell is close to the gland that made the hormone
Whether the cell expresses a receptor for that hormone
Whether the hormone is present at a high enough total concentration
Whether the cell has an open channel for the hormone to enter
cards.explanation: Blood carries hormone to every cell, so the receptor is what selects the target and gives endocrine signaling its specificity. Distance from the gland does not matter once a hormone is in the circulation. Concentration changes how strong the response is in cells that already have receptors, and hormones do not enter through channels.

cards.q: What decides the nature of the response a target cell makes to a hormone?
cards.a: The receptor and signaling machinery of the target cell.
options: The gland that secreted the hormone
The chemical structure of the hormone molecule by itself
The receptor and signaling machinery of the target cell
The distance the hormone traveled in the blood
cards.explanation: The hormone is only a key, and the response depends on what the cell it unlocks is equipped to do, which is why one molecule can trigger opposite effects in two tissues. The hormone structure determines which receptors it fits, not what those receptors then do. Travel distance and gland of origin have no bearing on the target cell's machinery.

cards.q: What does down regulation of a receptor mean?
cards.a: The target cell reduces the number of receptors for a hormone.
options: The gland decreases its secretion of the hormone
The receptor moves from the membrane into the nucleus instead
The hormone is broken down faster in the liver
The target cell reduces the number of receptors for a hormone
cards.explanation: Down regulation is a change in the target cell, which internalizes and degrades receptors so the same hormone concentration produces a smaller effect. Reduced secretion is a change in the gland and is a separate mechanism. Receptors do not migrate between the membrane and the nucleus, and faster hepatic breakdown changes hormone level rather than receptor number.

cards.q: Chronically elevated hormone levels usually produce which change in target cell receptors?
cards.a: Down regulation, so the cell becomes less sensitive.
options: Down regulation, so the cell becomes less sensitive
No change, since receptor number is fixed at birth
Conversion of surface receptors into intracellular receptors
Up regulation, so the cell becomes more sensitive
cards.explanation: Persistent high hormone drives receptor internalization and degradation, which protects the cell from overstimulation and is a common route into hormone resistance. Up regulation is the opposite response and follows chronically low hormone. Receptor number is continually adjusted rather than fixed, and receptor type does not switch locations.

cards.q: Chronically low hormone levels usually produce which change in the target cell?
cards.a: Up regulation, an increase in receptor number.
options: Down regulation, a decrease in receptor number
Up regulation, an increase in receptor number
Loss of the second messenger system
Permanent loss of the ability to respond
cards.explanation: When a signal is scarce the cell adds receptors so that whatever hormone does arrive produces a larger effect, which raises sensitivity. Down regulation is the response to excess rather than to scarcity. The second messenger system remains intact, and the change is reversible rather than permanent.

cards.q: If a target cell increases its number of receptors for a hormone, what happens to its sensitivity?
cards.a: Sensitivity increases, so a lower hormone concentration produces a given response.
options: Sensitivity is unchanged, since sensitivity depends only on hormone level
Sensitivity increases only if the hormone is lipid soluble
Sensitivity increases, so a lower hormone concentration produces a given response
Sensitivity decreases, so more hormone is needed for a given response
cards.explanation: More binding sites means more receptors are occupied at any given hormone concentration, so the dose response curve shifts left and less hormone is needed. Needing more hormone describes fewer receptors, not more. Sensitivity is a property of the target cell, and it responds to receptor number regardless of hormone class.

cards.q: Epinephrine constricts vessels in the skin and dilates vessels in skeletal muscle. What accounts for the opposite results?
cards.a: The two beds express different adrenergic receptor subtypes.
options: Epinephrine is chemically altered on its way to muscle
Muscle vessels have no receptors for epinephrine
Skin vessels receive a higher concentration of epinephrine
The two beds express different adrenergic receptor subtypes
cards.explanation: Skin arterioles are rich in alpha1 receptors that raise intracellular Ca2+ and constrict, while skeletal muscle arterioles carry beta2 receptors that raise cyclic AMP and relax the smooth muscle. Both beds see the same circulating concentration, since one blood supply serves both. The hormone is not modified en route, and muscle vessels clearly do respond, so they cannot lack receptors.

cards.q: A cell has no receptor for a hormone at all. What is its response to a high blood level of that hormone?
cards.a: No response, no matter how high the concentration goes.
options: No response, no matter how high the concentration goes
A response only if the hormone is lipid soluble
A delayed response after receptors diffuse in from neighbors
A weak response that grows with concentration
cards.explanation: Without a receptor there is nothing for the hormone to bind, so the signal is never transduced and raising the concentration adds nothing. A weak but growing response would require at least a few low affinity receptors. Lipid solubility lets a hormone enter the cell but it still needs an intracellular receptor, and receptors are not shared between cells.

cards.q: A person has had very high insulin levels for years. Predict the change in insulin receptor number and in target cell sensitivity.
cards.a: Receptor number falls and sensitivity decreases.
options: Receptor number rises and sensitivity increases
Receptor number falls and sensitivity decreases
Receptor number falls and sensitivity increases
Receptor number is unchanged and sensitivity decreases
cards.explanation: Sustained excess hormone triggers internalization and degradation of receptors, so fewer remain and a given insulin level does less, which is the core of insulin resistance. Rising receptor number is the answer to chronic hormone deficiency. A fall in receptors cannot raise sensitivity, and resistance in this setting is driven by the receptor change rather than occurring with receptor number held constant.

cards.q: Thyroid hormone increases the number of beta adrenergic receptors on cardiac muscle. Predict the effect of a fixed dose of epinephrine on heart rate in a person with excess thyroid hormone.
cards.a: A larger increase in heart rate than normal.
options: A fall in heart rate, since the receptors are saturated
A smaller increase in heart rate than normal
A larger increase in heart rate than normal
No change in heart rate at all
cards.explanation: More beta receptors means more of them are occupied at the same epinephrine concentration, so the cell is more sensitive and the chronotropic response is exaggerated, which is why thyroid excess produces palpitations. A smaller response would follow receptor down regulation. Adding receptors cannot abolish the response, and beta receptor activation raises heart rate rather than lowering it.

cards.q: A drug blocks only the beta2 receptor. Predict its effect on the response to epinephrine in skeletal muscle arterioles and in skin arterioles.
cards.a: Muscle dilation is blocked and skin constriction is preserved.
options: Skin constriction is blocked and muscle dilation is preserved
Neither response changes, since the hormone is unchanged
Both dilation and constriction are blocked
Muscle dilation is blocked and skin constriction is preserved
cards.explanation: A subtype selective blocker removes only the response that runs through that subtype, so beta2 mediated dilation in muscle is lost while alpha1 mediated constriction in skin continues. Blocking both would require a nonselective drug. Reversing the two mixes up which bed carries which subtype, and blocking a receptor changes the response even though the hormone level is normal.

cards.q: Two cells are exposed to the same concentration of a hormone. Cell A responds strongly, cell B barely responds. Both have the same second messenger system. What is the most likely explanation?
cards.a: Cell A has more receptors for that hormone than cell B.
options: Cell A has more receptors for that hormone than cell B
Cell A binds more of the hormone to carrier protein
Cell A is exposed to the hormone for a shorter time
Cell A is closer to the gland of origin
cards.explanation: With the same hormone concentration and the same downstream machinery, the number of binding sites is what sets how much signal gets in, so receptor density explains the difference in sensitivity. Distance from the gland is irrelevant once the hormone is in the blood. Carrier binding happens in plasma, not on target cells, and a shorter exposure would weaken rather than strengthen the response.

cards.q: A tumor secretes a large excess of a peptide hormone for many months, then is removed. Immediately after removal, target cells are likely to be
cards.a: less sensitive than normal, because receptors were down regulated.
options: more sensitive than normal, because receptors were up regulated
less sensitive than normal, because receptors were down regulated
unchanged, because receptor number responds only to hormone class
unable to respond ever again, because receptors were permanently lost
cards.explanation: Months of excess hormone leave the cells with a reduced receptor population, so once hormone levels fall the tissue underresponds until receptor number recovers over days. Up regulation follows deficiency, not excess. Receptor number tracks hormone exposure rather than hormone class, and the change reverses as the cell synthesizes new receptors.

cards.q: Glucagon raises cyclic AMP in a liver cell and epinephrine raises cyclic AMP in the same liver cell. Both produce glucose release. What does this show about specificity?
cards.a: Different receptors can converge on one second messenger.
options: The liver cell can only respond to one hormone at a time
The two hormones must bind the same receptor
Different receptors can converge on one second messenger
Cyclic AMP is specific to a single hormone in each cell
cards.explanation: Specificity lives at the receptor, but several receptors in one cell can feed the same amplifier, so two hormones with different receptors produce the same end result. They cannot share a receptor, since a receptor is selective for one hormone shape. Cyclic AMP is a general purpose messenger, and a cell can carry receptors for many hormones at once.

cards.q: Antidiuretic hormone contracts vascular smooth muscle through V1 receptors and inserts water channels in the collecting duct through V2 receptors. What is the best summary of why one hormone does two different things?
cards.a: Each tissue expresses a different receptor subtype and pathway.
options: The kidney receives the hormone at a much lower concentration
The two tissues receive the hormone by different routes
The hormone changes shape when it enters the kidney
Each tissue expresses a different receptor subtype and pathway
cards.explanation: Receptor subtype selects which intracellular pathway is opened, so the same molecule raises Ca2+ in smooth muscle and cyclic AMP in the collecting duct cell. The hormone itself is unchanged from tissue to tissue. Concentration alters the size of a response, not its nature, and both tissues are reached by the same blood.

cards.q: A patient with type 2 diabetes has a fasting insulin level well above normal but a high blood glucose. Explain the combination in terms of receptors.
cards.a: Target cells have down regulated insulin receptors, so high insulin does little.
options: Target cells have down regulated insulin receptors, so high insulin does little
Insulin receptors are up regulated, which makes cells oversensitive to glucose
Insulin is bound to carrier protein, so none of it reaches target cells
The pancreas is secreting an inactive form of insulin, so glucose stays high
cards.explanation: High hormone with a weak effect is the signature of reduced target sensitivity, and years of elevated insulin drive receptor down regulation, so glucose stays up even as the pancreas works harder. An inactive hormone would not be measured as insulin in the usual assay. Up regulation would lower glucose rather than raise it, and insulin circulates free rather than carrier bound.

cards.q: A researcher gives a low dose of epinephrine to a person at rest and measures a fall in total peripheral resistance. The same dose during a massive sympathetic discharge produces a rise. Which receptor idea best explains the reversal?
cards.a: Low doses mainly occupy beta2 receptors, while more agonist recruits alpha1.
options: Epinephrine changes into norepinephrine during sympathetic discharge
Low doses mainly occupy beta2 receptors, while more agonist recruits alpha1
Receptors are down regulated within seconds of the first dose
The blood carries epinephrine to different organs at rest than during stress
cards.explanation: Both receptor subtypes are present in the circulation wide vascular bed, and which effect wins depends on how many of each are occupied, so a small amount of agonist reveals the more easily occupied beta2 dilation while a flood recruits enough alpha1 to constrict. Epinephrine is not converted to norepinephrine in plasma. Down regulation takes hours, not seconds, and the distribution of blood flow does not change which receptors a vessel carries.

cards.q: A cell line is engineered to express the receptor for a hormone it normally ignores, with no other change. Predict what happens when the hormone is applied, and what that shows.
cards.a: The cell now responds, showing that receptor expression is what makes a cell a target.
options: The cell secretes the hormone itself, since receptor and secretion are linked
The cell still ignores the hormone, since the gland did not send it a signal
The cell now responds, showing that receptor expression is what makes a cell a target
The cell responds only if the hormone is lipid soluble
cards.explanation: Adding the receptor is sufficient to make a nontarget cell responsive, which is the clearest demonstration that targeting comes from the receptor rather than from anything about the hormone or the gland. There is no separate permission signal from the gland. Lipid solubility determines where the receptor must sit, not whether the experiment works, and receptor expression does not confer the ability to make the hormone.

cards.q: Cortisol is given at a high dose for two months and then stopped abruptly. Beyond the well known suppression of the axis, predict the receptor level change in target tissues and its effect during the first days after stopping.
cards.a: Down regulated glucocorticoid receptors leave the tissue underresponsive.
options: Receptor number is unchanged, since steroid receptors are not regulated
Receptors are converted to membrane receptors, which respond faster
Up regulated receptors make tissues oversensitive, causing signs of excess
Down regulated glucocorticoid receptors leave the tissue underresponsive
cards.explanation: Two months of excess hormone reduces receptor number in the target tissue, so when the drug stops the tissue is doubly short changed, once by low hormone from the suppressed axis and again by reduced sensitivity. Up regulation would follow deficiency rather than months of excess. Intracellular receptors are regulated like surface receptors, and receptors do not change location or class.

cards.q: What does synergism between two hormones mean?
cards.a: Their combined effect is greater than the sum of their separate effects.
options: Their combined effect is greater than the sum of their separate effects
One hormone must be present for the other to act at all
One hormone opposes the effect of the other
Their combined effect is exactly the sum of their separate effects
cards.explanation: Synergism means the two together produce more than simple addition, usually because they act at different points of the same pathway and amplify one another. Requiring one hormone to be present for the other is permissiveness. Opposition is antagonism, and exact addition is an additive effect, which is the baseline that synergism exceeds.

cards.q: What does permissiveness between two hormones mean?
cards.a: One hormone must be present for the second to exert its full effect.
options: The two hormones together produce more than the sum of their effects
One hormone must be present for the second to exert its full effect
The two hormones cancel each other out completely
The two hormones bind the same receptor with equal affinity
cards.explanation: A permissive hormone does little on its own but sets the stage, often by increasing the number of receptors or enzymes the second hormone needs. More than additive effect describes synergism, in which both hormones produce an effect on their own. Cancellation is antagonism, and permissiveness does not require the two to share a receptor.

cards.q: What does antagonism between two hormones mean?
cards.a: One hormone opposes or reduces the effect of the other.
options: The two hormones produce a greater than additive effect
The two hormones are secreted by the same gland
One hormone opposes or reduces the effect of the other
The two hormones must both be present for any effect
cards.explanation: In antagonism the net effect on a variable is smaller than what either hormone would produce alone, either because they drive it in opposite directions or because one blunts the other's receptor. Requiring both for any effect is permissiveness. Greater than additive is synergism, and being secreted by the same gland says nothing about how the effects combine.

cards.q: Thyroid hormone increases the number of beta receptors so that epinephrine can raise heart rate normally. Which interaction is that?
cards.a: Permissiveness.
options: Antagonism
Additive effect
Synergism
Permissiveness
cards.explanation: Thyroid hormone does not itself produce the catecholamine response but is required for the full response to occur, which is the definition of a permissive hormone, and it works here by raising receptor number. Synergism would require thyroid hormone to produce the same effect on its own and for the pair to exceed addition. Antagonism would reduce the epinephrine effect, and an additive effect requires two independent contributions.

cards.q: Insulin lowers blood glucose while glucagon raises it. Which interaction do the two show?
cards.a: Antagonism.
options: Antagonism
Additive effect
Permissiveness
Synergism
cards.explanation: The two hormones move the same variable in opposite directions, so the net blood glucose reflects their ratio rather than either level alone, which is the essence of antagonism. Permissiveness would mean one enables the other. Synergism and an additive effect both require the two to push in the same direction.

cards.q: Glucagon, cortisol, and epinephrine together raise blood glucose far more than the sum of what each raises alone. Which interaction is that?
cards.a: Synergism.
options: Additive effect
Synergism
Antagonism
Permissiveness
cards.explanation: Exceeding the sum of the separate effects is the defining test for synergism, and it happens here because the three hormones act on different steps of glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis at once. Antagonism would predict a smaller combined effect. Permissiveness applies when one hormone alone does nothing, and an additive effect stops exactly at the sum.

cards.q: Cortisol is required for vascular smooth muscle to constrict normally in response to norepinephrine, though cortisol itself is not a vasoconstrictor. What is cortisol acting as here?
cards.a: A permissive hormone.
options: A trophic hormone
A synergistic hormone
A permissive hormone
An antagonistic hormone
cards.explanation: Cortisol produces no constriction on its own but the response to norepinephrine is weak without it, which is the classic permissive pattern and part of why cortisol deficiency causes low blood pressure. Synergism requires both partners to produce the effect independently. Antagonism would weaken the constriction, and a trophic hormone is one that stimulates another endocrine gland.

cards.q: Estrogen increases the number of progesterone receptors in the uterus so that progesterone can act. What does this illustrate?
cards.a: A permissive effect achieved by up regulating receptors.
options: An antagonistic effect achieved by blocking receptors
A synergistic effect on the same receptor
A direct additive effect on endometrial growth
A permissive effect achieved by up regulating receptors
cards.explanation: Priming a tissue by raising receptor number is one of the commonest mechanisms of permissiveness, since the second hormone cannot act until the receptors exist. Blocking receptors would be antagonism, the opposite of what estrogen does here. Synergism would require both hormones to act through one shared pathway beyond addition, and this is an enabling step rather than an independent contribution.

cards.q: Hormone A alone raises a measured response by 10 units, hormone B alone by 10 units, and the two together by 45 units. Which interaction is this?
cards.a: Synergism.
options: Synergism
Permissiveness
Antagonism
Additive effect
cards.explanation: Addition would predict 20 units, and 45 is far above that, so the two hormones amplify each other rather than simply summing. Permissiveness would show one hormone producing little or nothing alone, but here each produces 10 units. Antagonism would give a combined value below 20.

cards.q: Hormone C alone raises a response by 0 units, hormone D alone by 5 units, and the two together by 30 units. Which interaction is this?
cards.a: Permissiveness.
options: Additive effect
Permissiveness
Synergism
Antagonism
cards.explanation: Hormone C does nothing on its own yet the response to hormone D is six times larger in its presence, which is the signature of a permissive hormone that prepares the tissue. Antagonism would lower the combined response below 5 units. An additive effect would give 5 units, and synergism is usually reserved for pairs that each produce a measurable effect alone.

cards.q: A patient cannot make cortisol and has a dangerously low blood pressure that responds poorly to injected norepinephrine. Which interaction explains the poor response?
cards.a: Loss of the permissive action of cortisol on vascular responsiveness.
options: Synergism between cortisol and aldosterone on the kidney
Down regulation of cortisol receptors by norepinephrine
Loss of the permissive action of cortisol on vascular responsiveness
Antagonism between cortisol and norepinephrine at the same receptor
cards.explanation: Cortisol is required for vascular smooth muscle to respond fully to catecholamines, so when it is absent the same dose of norepinephrine produces far less constriction. If the two were antagonists, removing cortisol would improve rather than worsen the response. The aldosterone pairing is a different interaction and does not explain the failure of injected norepinephrine, and norepinephrine does not regulate cortisol receptors here.

cards.q: Parathyroid hormone raises plasma Ca2+ and calcitonin lowers it. Which term describes this pair?
cards.a: Antagonists.
options: Synergists
Trophic partners
Permissive partners
Antagonists
cards.explanation: The two hormones act on the same variable in opposite directions, so plasma Ca2+ settles where their opposing effects balance. Permissiveness would require one to enable the other. Synergism means pushing the same way beyond addition, and neither hormone stimulates the other's gland, which is what trophic would mean.

cards.q: In an animal with no thyroid hormone, growth hormone alone produces almost no growth, but growth hormone plus thyroid hormone produces normal growth. Which interaction is shown?
cards.a: Permissiveness of thyroid hormone for growth hormone.
options: Permissiveness of thyroid hormone for growth hormone
Synergism in which each hormone alone produces normal growth
Additive growth from two independent pathways
Antagonism of growth hormone by thyroid hormone
cards.explanation: Growth hormone cannot act fully unless thyroid hormone has prepared the tissues, so removing thyroid hormone leaves growth hormone almost ineffective, which is permissiveness. Antagonism would predict better growth without thyroid hormone. The synergism option contradicts the data, since growth hormone alone did almost nothing, and independent additive pathways would still give partial growth.

cards.q: A drug blocks the glucagon receptor in the liver of a fasting person. Predict the effect on blood glucose and name the interaction that is disturbed.
cards.a: Blood glucose falls, because the antagonism that balanced insulin is removed.
options: Blood glucose rises, because insulin action is also blocked
Blood glucose falls, because the antagonism that balanced insulin is removed
Blood glucose is unchanged, because cortisol replaces glucagon exactly
Blood glucose falls, because glucagon and insulin are synergists
cards.explanation: Glucose sits where the opposing actions of insulin and glucagon balance, so removing glucagon action lets insulin dominate and glucose drops. Blocking the glucagon receptor does not block insulin. Cortisol contributes to glucose production but slowly and not in exact replacement, and calling the pair synergists misnames a relationship in which they push in opposite directions.

cards.q: An animal without adrenal glands is given epinephrine and shows a weak rise in blood glucose. It is then given cortisol for two days, and the same epinephrine dose now produces a large rise. Identify the interaction and its likely mechanism.
cards.a: Permissiveness, with cortisol raising the enzymes epinephrine needs.
options: Additive effect, with each hormone contributing an independent share
Antagonism, with cortisol competing for the adrenergic receptor
Permissiveness, with cortisol raising the enzymes epinephrine needs
Synergism, with both hormones acting on the same receptor at once
cards.explanation: Cortisol pretreatment did not itself produce the glucose surge but made the epinephrine response much larger, which is the permissive pattern, and cortisol accomplishes it by increasing gluconeogenic enzymes and adrenergic receptor number. Antagonism would blunt the response after cortisol. Synergism requires both hormones to raise glucose on their own, and an additive effect would not multiply the epinephrine response the way this experiment shows.

cards.q: During a long fast, glucagon, cortisol, growth hormone, and epinephrine all rise while insulin falls. Explain what the two arrangements of interaction accomplish for blood glucose.
cards.a: The four raise glucose synergistically while their antagonist insulin falls.
options: The four hormones are permissive for insulin, which is what raises glucose
The four hormones antagonize each other, which is why glucose stays constant
All five hormones are synergists whose effects sum to a stable glucose level
The four raise glucose synergistically while their antagonist insulin falls
cards.explanation: Glucose is defended by two moves at once, more of the hormones that mobilize fuel and less of the hormone that stores it, and the mobilizers together exceed the sum of their individual effects. Insulin cannot be grouped with the other four, since it lowers glucose. Insulin does not raise glucose, and calling the four mutual antagonists would predict no net rise during a fast.

cards.q: Two hormones each raise heart rate. Given alone, hormone E raises rate by 12 beats per minute and hormone F by 8. Together they raise it by 20. A student calls this synergism. What is the correct label and why?
cards.a: An additive effect, because the total equals the sum of the two rises.
options: An additive effect, because the total equals the sum of the two rises
Permissiveness, because both hormones were required for the full effect
Antagonism, because the increase is smaller than either hormone alone
Synergism, because two hormones acting together is always more than one
cards.explanation: Synergism requires the combination to exceed the sum, and 20 is exactly 12 plus 8, so these hormones simply add through independent routes. The number of hormones present does not by itself make an interaction synergistic. Permissiveness would show one hormone producing little alone, and antagonism would give a combined value below 12.

cards.q: A patient on a drug that blocks estrogen receptors is given progesterone and the uterine response is much smaller than expected. Trace why, and identify the interaction that was interrupted.
cards.a: Blocking estrogen prevented up regulation of progesterone receptors, a permissive effect.
options: Blocking estrogen removed an antagonist, so progesterone should have acted more strongly
Blocking estrogen prevented up regulation of progesterone receptors, a permissive effect
Progesterone and estrogen are synergists at a shared receptor that the drug blocked
The drug lowered plasma progesterone by displacing it from its carrier protein
cards.explanation: Estrogen primes the endometrium by increasing progesterone receptor number, so with estrogen receptors blocked there are too few progesterone receptors and the same hormone level does much less. If estrogen were an antagonist here, blocking it would have amplified the progesterone effect. The two hormones use separate receptors rather than one shared site, and a receptor blocker does not change plasma carrier binding.

cards.q: What defines a humoral stimulus for hormone release?
cards.a: A change in the blood level of an ion or nutrient acts on the gland.
options: A stretch receptor in a hollow organ is activated
A nerve fiber releases neurotransmitter directly onto the gland cells
A change in the blood level of an ion or nutrient acts on the gland
Another hormone binds receptors on the gland
cards.explanation: Humoral refers to the body fluids, so the stimulus is the concentration of something dissolved in blood, such as glucose or Ca2+, sensed by the endocrine cell itself. Neurotransmitter release onto a gland is a neural stimulus, and another hormone acting on the gland is a hormonal stimulus. A stretch receptor generates a neural signal rather than a humoral one.

cards.q: What defines a neural stimulus for hormone release?
cards.a: A neuron releases neurotransmitter onto the endocrine cells.
options: A rise in plasma K+ acts on the gland
A pituitary trophic hormone acts on the gland
The gland responds to a fall in blood pressure entirely by itself
A neuron releases neurotransmitter onto the endocrine cells
cards.explanation: In a neural stimulus the gland is innervated and the action potential arriving at the nerve ending triggers secretion, which gives the fastest possible endocrine response. A rise in plasma K+ is a humoral stimulus sensed by the cell itself. A trophic hormone is a hormonal stimulus, and a gland detecting a blood variable on its own is humoral.

cards.q: What defines a hormonal stimulus for hormone release?
cards.a: One hormone stimulates an endocrine gland to release a second hormone.
options: One hormone stimulates an endocrine gland to release a second hormone
A sympathetic nerve fires onto the gland
The gland releases hormone at a fixed rate regardless of signals
A blood ion level changes and the gland responds
cards.explanation: A hormonal stimulus is hormone acting on hormone, the arrangement that builds the three tier axes of the hypothalamus and pituitary. Ion driven release is humoral and nerve driven release is neural. Constant unregulated release is not one of the three categories and is not how endocrine glands behave.

cards.q: A rise in blood glucose triggers insulin secretion from the pancreatic beta cell. Which type of stimulus is that?
cards.a: Humoral.
options: Neural
Humoral
Hormonal
Trophic
cards.explanation: The beta cell senses glucose directly from the blood, so the nutrient itself is the stimulus, which is the definition of humoral. A neural stimulus would require nerve fibers to drive the secretion, and although autonomic nerves modulate the islet, glucose is the primary signal. There is no intervening hormone, so it is not hormonal or trophic.

cards.q: A fall in plasma Ca2+ triggers parathyroid hormone release. Which type of stimulus is that?
cards.a: Humoral.
options: Hormonal
Neural
Humoral
Neuroendocrine reflex
cards.explanation: The parathyroid chief cell carries a calcium sensing receptor and reads plasma Ca2+ directly, so the ion in the blood is the stimulus. No other hormone stands between the change and the secretion, which rules out a hormonal stimulus. Nothing neural is involved, so neither of the nerve based options fits.

cards.q: Sympathetic preganglionic fibers release acetylcholine onto adrenal medullary cells, which then secrete epinephrine. Which type of stimulus is that?
cards.a: Neural.
options: Paracrine
Humoral
Hormonal
Neural
cards.explanation: The medulla is effectively a modified sympathetic ganglion, and its secretory cells fire in response to neurotransmitter from a preganglionic neuron, which is a neural stimulus and explains the near instant catecholamine surge. No blood borne ion or nutrient triggers it, so it is not humoral, and no other hormone acts on the gland. Paracrine signaling is local diffusion between neighboring cells rather than a neural pathway.

cards.q: ACTH from the anterior pituitary triggers cortisol release from the adrenal cortex. Which type of stimulus is that?
cards.a: Hormonal.
options: Hormonal
Humoral
Neural
Mechanical
cards.explanation: One hormone acting on another endocrine gland is a hormonal stimulus, and ACTH is the trophic hormone that drives the adrenal cortex. Humoral would require the cortex to be sensing an ion or nutrient. Nerve fibers do not drive cortisol secretion, and there is no mechanical trigger in this pathway.

cards.q: Which stimulus type produces the fastest hormone secretion after the trigger appears?
cards.a: Neural.
options: Hormonal
Neural
All three act at the same speed
Humoral
cards.explanation: A neural stimulus travels by action potential and releases a preformed vesicle pool within seconds, which is why the adrenal medulla can respond to a startle almost immediately. A humoral stimulus waits for a blood level to change enough for the gland to sense it. A hormonal stimulus adds an entire extra gland and transit time, making it the slowest of the three.

cards.q: Plasma K+ rises and the adrenal cortex secretes more aldosterone. Classify the stimulus.
cards.a: Humoral, because the ion acts on the gland directly.
options: Hormonal, because K+ acts through renin
Neural, because K+ depolarizes nerve endings on the gland
Humoral, because the ion acts on the gland directly
Hormonal, because K+ acts through ACTH
cards.explanation: Zona glomerulosa cells are depolarized directly by extracellular K+, which is why potassium is one of the strongest aldosterone stimuli and needs no intermediary. The depolarization happens in the endocrine cell rather than in a nerve. ACTH has only a permissive role for aldosterone, and while renin drives the angiotensin route, potassium acts on the gland without it.

cards.q: Suckling at the breast leads to oxytocin release from the posterior pituitary. Classify the stimulus.
cards.a: Neural, since sensory nerves drive the hypothalamic neurons.
options: Hormonal, since prolactin release triggers oxytocin release from the gland
Humoral, since the fall in plasma volume triggers it
Humoral, since milk components enter the blood
Neural, since sensory nerves drive the hypothalamic neurons
cards.explanation: Mechanoreceptors in the nipple send action potentials to the hypothalamus, and the hypothalamic neurons release oxytocin from their endings in the posterior pituitary, so the whole loop is neural. Nothing dissolved in blood is being sensed, which rules out both humoral options. Prolactin is released by the same reflex but does not itself trigger oxytocin.

cards.q: TSH from the pituitary raises thyroid hormone output. Classify the stimulus acting on the thyroid gland.
cards.a: Hormonal.
options: Hormonal
Neurohumoral
Neural
Humoral
cards.explanation: The thyroid follicular cell is responding to a hormone from another endocrine gland, which is the hormonal category by definition. It is not sensing an ion or nutrient in the blood, so humoral does not apply, even though iodine availability limits how much hormone it can make. No nerve fiber drives thyroid hormone secretion.

cards.q: A student says that a hormone circulating in the blood makes any stimulus that reaches a gland through blood a humoral stimulus. Why is that wrong?
cards.a: Humoral covers blood levels of ions and nutrients, not hormone on gland.
options: Humoral applies only to stimuli sensed in the hypothalamus
Humoral covers blood levels of ions and nutrients, not hormone on gland
Humoral applies only to stimuli that arrive through lymph rather than blood
Humoral applies only when the gland is also innervated
cards.explanation: The three categories are defined by what kind of signal reaches the gland, not by the route it traveled, so a hormone arriving through blood is still a hormonal stimulus. Lymph is not the defining route for any of the categories. Innervation would make the stimulus neural, and the hypothalamus is one site of sensing among many rather than a requirement.

cards.q: Blood glucose falls during a fast and the alpha cell secretes glucagon. Classify the stimulus and name what the gland is sensing.
cards.a: Humoral, sensing the plasma glucose concentration.
options: Humoral, sensing the plasma Ca2+ concentration
Neural, sensing sympathetic activity to the pancreas
Humoral, sensing the plasma glucose concentration
Hormonal, sensing the fall in plasma insulin
cards.explanation: The alpha cell reads the nutrient level in blood directly, which is a humoral stimulus and lets the pancreas respond to fuel status without waiting for any other signal. Sympathetic input does modulate the islet during stress but is not the primary trigger during a simple fast. Falling insulin contributes but is not what the alpha cell is chiefly sensing, and Ca2+ is the humoral stimulus for the parathyroid rather than the alpha cell.

cards.q: Which pathway would still work in an animal whose nerves to the endocrine gland have all been cut, with everything else intact?
cards.a: Low plasma Ca2+ raising parathyroid hormone.
options: Suckling raising oxytocin from the posterior pituitary
Cold air on the skin raising sympathetic output
A startle raising epinephrine from the adrenal medulla
Low plasma Ca2+ raising parathyroid hormone
cards.explanation: A humoral pathway needs only the blood and the gland, so parathyroid hormone release continues when the nerve supply is gone. The startle response and the suckling reflex both begin with sensory nerves and end with neural drive to secretory cells, so cutting nerves abolishes them. Cold sensing and sympathetic output are neural from start to finish.

cards.q: After a meal, glucose from the gut raises insulin, and gut derived GIP raises it further. Classify these two stimuli on the beta cell.
cards.a: Glucose is a humoral stimulus and GIP is a hormonal stimulus.
options: Glucose is a humoral stimulus and GIP is a hormonal stimulus
Glucose is a hormonal stimulus and GIP is a neural stimulus
Both glucose and GIP are neural stimuli
Both glucose and GIP are humoral stimuli
cards.explanation: One gland can receive more than one category of stimulus, and here the beta cell senses a nutrient directly, which is humoral, while GIP is a hormone from another endocrine tissue acting on it, which is hormonal. Calling GIP humoral misses that the category depends on what kind of signal arrives, not on the fact that it traveled in blood. Glucose is a nutrient rather than a hormone, and neither signal involves a nerve ending.

cards.q: Trace the full pathway from a frightening sight to epinephrine in the blood, and name the stimulus category at the gland.
cards.a: Brain to sympathetic preganglionic neuron to adrenal medullary cell, a neural stimulus.
options: Brain to hypothalamic releasing hormone to pituitary to adrenal medulla, a hormonal stimulus
Brain to sympathetic preganglionic neuron to adrenal medullary cell, a neural stimulus
Rising plasma glucose to adrenal medullary cell, a humoral stimulus
Brain to ACTH to adrenal medullary cell, a hormonal stimulus
cards.explanation: The medulla is innervated directly by sympathetic preganglionic fibers, so the signal never leaves the nervous system until acetylcholine triggers catecholamine exocytosis, which is why the response takes seconds. The hypothalamic pituitary route is the cortisol pathway and is far slower. Glucose does not drive medullary secretion, and ACTH acts on the adrenal cortex rather than the medulla.

cards.q: Trace the pathway from a low blood Ca2+ to a corrected Ca2+, and identify the stimulus category and the feedback sign.
cards.a: Low Ca2+ acts humorally on the parathyroid, PTH raises Ca2+, and that shuts off PTH.
options: Low Ca2+ triggers TSH, which raises PTH, and the rise in Ca2+ raises PTH further
Low Ca2+ acts humorally on the thyroid, calcitonin raises Ca2+, and the rise shuts off calcitonin
Low Ca2+ acts humorally on the parathyroid, PTH raises Ca2+, and that shuts off PTH
Low Ca2+ acts neurally on the parathyroid, PTH lowers Ca2+, and the fall shuts off PTH
cards.explanation: The chief cell reads plasma Ca2+ directly, PTH pulls Ca2+ from bone and kidney and gut, and the restored Ca2+ removes the stimulus, which is a simple negative feedback loop with a humoral trigger. PTH raises rather than lowers Ca2+, and the parathyroid is not driven by nerves. TSH controls the thyroid, not the parathyroid, and calcitonin lowers Ca2+ rather than raising it.

cards.q: An experimental animal has its pituitary stalk cut, blocking hypothalamic hormones from reaching the anterior pituitary. Which secretion is least affected, and why?
cards.a: Insulin, because it is driven by a humoral stimulus alone.
options: Thyroid hormone, because the thyroid is controlled by a neural stimulus
Sex steroids, because the gonads respond to plasma glucose
Cortisol, because the adrenal cortex is directly innervated
Insulin, because it is driven by a humoral stimulus alone
cards.explanation: Cutting the stalk removes the hormonal drive to the anterior pituitary, which cripples every three tier axis, but insulin secretion depends on the beta cell sensing glucose and is untouched. Cortisol falls because ACTH falls, and the cortex is not driven by nerves. The thyroid depends on TSH rather than nerves, and the gonads respond to LH and FSH rather than to glucose.

cards.q: A person eats a meal that is high in protein. Insulin and glucagon both rise. Classify the stimulus for each and explain why raising both makes sense.
cards.a: Both are humoral responses to amino acids, and the pair protects blood glucose.
options: Both are humoral responses to amino acids, and the pair protects blood glucose
Insulin is humoral and glucagon is neural, and the pair raises blood glucose sharply
Both are neural responses to gastric stretch, and the pair slows digestion
Both are hormonal responses to a gut trophic hormone that raises glucose
cards.explanation: Amino acids in the blood are sensed directly by both islet cell types, so both signals are humoral, and glucagon offsets the hypoglycemia that a large insulin release without carbohydrate would otherwise cause. Gut hormones such as GIP amplify insulin release but are not the main trigger here and do not raise glucose. Glucagon secretion is not primarily neural, and gastric stretch does not account for the amino acid response.

cards.q: How do hypothalamic releasing hormones reach the anterior pituitary?
cards.a: Through the hypophyseal portal veins.
options: By diffusion across the blood brain barrier
Through the hypophyseal portal veins
Through the general systemic circulation from the heart
Down the axons of hypothalamic neurons into the anterior lobe
cards.explanation: A portal system carries blood from a capillary bed in the hypothalamus straight to a second capillary bed in the anterior pituitary, so tiny amounts of releasing hormone arrive undiluted. Going through the systemic circulation would dilute them past usefulness. Axonal transport into the lobe describes the posterior pituitary, and these hormones do not need to cross the blood brain barrier on this route.

cards.q: In a three tier axis, which tier is the peripheral gland?
cards.a: The third tier, such as the thyroid or adrenal cortex.
options: The first tier, the hypothalamus and its releasing neurons
The second tier, the anterior pituitary and its trophic cells
The third tier, such as the thyroid or adrenal cortex
The posterior pituitary, which stores hypothalamic hormones
cards.explanation: The axis runs hypothalamus, then anterior pituitary, then peripheral gland, and it is the peripheral gland that makes the hormone with the widespread effects on body tissues. The hypothalamus is tier one and releases the releasing hormone. The anterior pituitary is tier two and releases the trophic hormone, and the posterior pituitary is not part of a three tier axis at all.

cards.q: Which hormone does the anterior pituitary release in response to TRH?
cards.a: TSH.
options: ACTH
Calcitonin
Thyroxine
TSH
cards.explanation: TRH from the hypothalamus drives thyroid stimulating hormone from the anterior pituitary, which then drives the thyroid. Thyroxine is the third tier hormone from the thyroid gland itself. ACTH is the trophic hormone for the adrenal cortex and is driven by CRH, and calcitonin comes from thyroid parafollicular cells outside this axis.

cards.q: Trace the adrenal axis in the correct order.
cards.a: CRH, then ACTH, then cortisol.
options: CRH, then ACTH, then cortisol
CRH, then cortisol, then ACTH
ACTH, then cortisol, then CRH
ACTH, then CRH, then cortisol
cards.explanation: Corticotropin releasing hormone comes from the hypothalamus, drives ACTH from the anterior pituitary, and ACTH drives cortisol from the adrenal cortex. Putting ACTH first reverses the top two tiers. The other two orders place the peripheral hormone before its own trophic hormone, which would mean the gland acts before being told to.

cards.q: What is long loop negative feedback in a three tier axis?
cards.a: The peripheral hormone inhibits the hypothalamus and pituitary.
options: The trophic hormone inhibits the hypothalamus one tier above it
The peripheral hormone inhibits the hypothalamus and pituitary
The releasing hormone inhibits its own hypothalamic neurons
The peripheral gland hormone stimulates more trophic hormone
cards.explanation: Long loop means the signal travels the full length of the axis, from the third tier back up to tiers one and two, which is what keeps the peripheral hormone near its set point. A trophic hormone acting back on the hypothalamus is the short loop, a shorter journey. Releasing hormone acting on its own neurons is an ultrashort loop, and a stimulating effect from the third tier would be positive rather than negative feedback.

cards.q: What is short loop negative feedback in a three tier axis?
cards.a: The trophic hormone from the pituitary inhibits the hypothalamus.
options: The releasing hormone inhibits the peripheral gland
The peripheral hormone inhibits the anterior pituitary corticotrophs
The trophic hormone from the pituitary inhibits the hypothalamus
The peripheral hormone inhibits the hypothalamus
cards.explanation: The short loop skips the peripheral gland, with tier two feeding back on tier one so the pituitary can restrain its own drive. Any answer in which the peripheral hormone inhibits a tier above it describes long loop feedback instead. Releasing hormone acting on the peripheral gland is not a feedback path, since portal blood delivers it to the pituitary rather than to the periphery.

cards.q: Which pair correctly names a hypothalamic hormone and the anterior pituitary hormone it controls?
cards.a: GnRH and LH.
options: CRH and TSH
GHRH and ACTH
TRH and cortisol
GnRH and LH
cards.explanation: Gonadotropin releasing hormone drives the gonadotropins LH and FSH from the anterior pituitary, which then act on the gonads. CRH drives ACTH rather than TSH, and GHRH drives growth hormone rather than ACTH. Cortisol is a peripheral gland hormone and is not released by the pituitary at all.

cards.q: Why is the posterior pituitary not the middle tier of a three tier axis?
cards.a: It releases hormones that hypothalamic neurons made and sent down axons.
options: It releases hormones that hypothalamic neurons made and sent down axons
It receives releasing hormones through the portal system
It is controlled by long loop feedback from the adrenal cortex
It makes its own trophic hormones that drive peripheral glands
cards.explanation: Antidiuretic hormone and oxytocin are synthesized in hypothalamic cell bodies and travel down axons to be released from the posterior lobe, so there is no separate gland taking orders and no trophic step. The posterior lobe synthesizes no hormones of its own. The portal system serves the anterior lobe, and the adrenal cortex feeds back on the CRH and ACTH pathway rather than on the posterior pituitary.

cards.q: A drug destroys the hypophyseal portal vessels without damaging either the hypothalamus or the pituitary. Predict the effect on ACTH secretion.
cards.a: ACTH falls, because CRH can no longer reach the corticotrophs.
options: ACTH rises, because feedback from cortisol is removed
ACTH falls, because CRH can no longer reach the corticotrophs
ACTH is unchanged, because CRH travels down axons to the pituitary
ACTH rises, because the pituitary secretes freely without hypothalamic input
